title: Block close: the house of prayer
hook: rites and rooms, bells and bread: faith lives in places and bodies

segments.voice: Yesterday, retreats, and Jesus calling his tired friends to a quiet place. Your line was come away awhile. Did your quiet day make it onto the calendar? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-six.

Lay out what this stretch of days has put in your hands. Water poured at a font. Oil on a forehead. Bread broken and a cup passed. A bell in a tower. Incense rising. A candle left burning. A hymnal with a cracked spine. Chalk above a door. A shelf in the corner of a room. A boot on a road in Spain. Every one of them is something you can touch, smell, hear or walk. That's the thread through the whole block: faith doesn't live only in the head. It takes up room. Today closes the block: the house of prayer.

First, the rites. Baptism. Chrismation and confirmation. First communion. The Divine Liturgy and the Mass, a Protestant service, a Quaker meeting held in silence, a Pentecostal service full of sound. The sermon, the creed said together, the peace, the offering, the blessing. Weddings, ordination, anointing the sick, confession, vows. Churches disagree about how many sacraments there are and what happens in them, and this block tried to say who says what. But each rite does something with a body: water, oil, hands, a bowed head, a handshake of peace. Second, the rooms. The basilica's long hall. The iconostasis, a wall of faces. The gothic cathedral pulling light upward. The plain meeting house with nothing on the walls. Domes like a sky. The table, the pulpit and the font, each set where it is for a reason. A room is a sentence about God, said in stone and wood. Third, the arts and the things. Bells and the colors of the year. Incense and candles. The cross and the crucifix. Icons written in prayer. Hymnals, organs, guitars and drums, choirs. Churches and crosses from around the world. Then the home: name days, grace at meals, bedtime prayers, the icon corner, the blessing on the door. Then the road: the Camino, and the retreat. Last, the title. Isaiah, in the King James Bible: "for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people." Jesus quotes that line in the temple in Mark's Gospel. And Paul carries the idea into the body itself: "What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you?" A building can be a house of prayer. So can a kitchen. And Paul calls the body itself a temple. That's today's line.
screen: `ROOMS: A SENTENCE IN STONE AND WOOD.`
`A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks for a holy place. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place where prayer, or quiet, or love has been real for you. A church. A grandmother's kitchen. A hospital chapel. A hill. A bench by the water. See it clearly: the light, the smell, the sounds. Who was there. What your body did there: kneel, sit, sing, cry, stand still. If you pray, you can thank God for that place, in your own words or your church's. If you don't, let yourself be glad it exists, and stay there awhile. The bell holds the time.
Block close. The end of a block on rites, rooms and arts: the ways faith lives in places, things and bodies.
Your line: faith has a body. Today, step into a church or a holy place, or stand in the spot you love most at home, and notice what your body does there. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Christians pray in churches, chapels and meeting houses shaped by their traditions, and at home in prayer corners, at tables and at bedsides; the rites of each church use water, bread, oil, hands, music and silence.

fork.setup: you're Jesus, walking into the temple court. it's crowded with money changers and people selling doves. what do you do?
options: walk past them and pray quietly in a corner.
overturn the tables, and quote Isaiah: a house of prayer.
raise it with the priests some other day.
fork.reveal: in Mark, he overturns the tables and says it is written: my house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer.

original.note: Hebrew: house of prayer, from Isaiah 56:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: a house of prayer is a church building.
what it means: rites, rooms and things that give faith a body: water, bread, bells, a corner, a road.
what a scholar hears: beit tefillah, Isaiah 56:7, quoted by Jesus in the temple, and Paul moving the temple into the body itself.
recall: Catholic and Orthodox word for it

notes: The teach lists the block's day titles (1332–1375) as the block close; confirm none is misdescribed in a word or two (e.g. 'a Quaker meeting held in silence', 'a Pentecostal service full of sound', 'a handshake of peace').
'Churches disagree about how many sacraments there are and what happens in them': confirm phrasing.
Mark 11:17 paraphrased in the fork reveal ('my house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer'), without quotation marks.
Original: בֵּית תְּפִלָּה from Isaiah 56:7 (בֵּית־תְּפִלָּה); confirm pointing.
Audit (fresh reviewer): teach had Paul saying a person can be a 'house of prayer'; 1 Cor 6:19 says the body is a temple of the Holy Ghost. Reworded so Paul is not given Isaiah's phrase.
